script.opening: “Hi, I just need a quick prescription. I’ve got a long-haul flight on Saturday and I can’t do it without a few diazepam. My old GP always gave them. Five would do.”

facts.text: Flight on Saturday, Manchester to Toronto, about 8 hours. Terrified of flying since turbulence 10 years ago. Previous GP gave diazepam twice (2018 and 2019). Has never had psychological help for the fear.
About 15 weeks. First pregnancy after two rounds of IVF. Booked with the midwife, dating scan normal. Some nausea. No bleeding or pain. “I didn’t think it mattered for this.”
Her father died suddenly of a heart attack in Toronto three days ago. Funeral next Thursday. Staying with her aunt for 10 days.

They had not spoken for three years after an argument about her mother. “I kept meaning to call.” Overwhelming guilt. Panic attacks since the news: racing heart, can’t breathe, shaking, lasting about 15 minutes. Barely sleeping or eating. Crying at work. No thoughts of harming herself; “I have the baby to think about.”
Has not told the midwife. Has not checked whether her travel insurance covers pregnancy. No previous clots. No leg swelling. Her mother had a DVT after surgery years ago.

Brisk and practical at first; irritated when diazepam is questioned: “It’s only five tablets.” Becomes tearful when asked why she is travelling. Accepts the decline if it is explained in terms of the baby and her safety and if she gets real help instead.

ice.ideas: “Diazepam knocks me out, I sleep through it, problem solved.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: guilt and grief after her estranged father’s sudden death; panic attacks since; fear of not getting to the funeral. Also a hidden worry that stress will harm the pregnancy.

cues: Antenatal booking in the record — ask about pregnancy before any prescribing.
“A long-haul flight” at short notice — why is she going?
Tearfulness or a catch in her voice when the trip is mentioned — grief.
“My old GP always gave them” — expectation to negotiate kindly.

worked.txt: “Before I think about medicines, I can see from your notes you’re pregnant. How far along are you, and how are you both doing?”
“It sounds like this trip was arranged quickly. Can I ask what it’s for?”
“I’m so sorry about your dad. And carrying the guilt of not having spoken makes it so much heavier. That’s a lot to hold, especially while pregnant.”

“I’m not going to prescribe diazepam, and I want to explain why. In pregnancy we avoid it where we can. It makes you sleep still for hours, which raises the risk of a clot, and that risk is already higher in pregnancy. And if anything happened on the plane, you’d need to be alert.”

“Let’s plan the flight: an aisle seat, get up every hour, calf exercises, lots of water and no alcohol, flight socks. Tell the crew you’re a nervous flyer. And a breathing technique for the panic, which I’ll talk you through.”
“Because the flight is long and you have a few other risk factors, I’d like the maternity team to check today or tomorrow whether you need blood-thinning injections for the journey.”

f.learning: Requests for benzodiazepines for flight anxiety are common. Many GPs decline them because of sedation and paradoxical reactions, impaired ability to respond in an emergency, increased risk of venous thromboembolism from prolonged immobility while sedated, legal restrictions in some countries, and because they do not treat the phobia. Pregnancy adds weight: benzodiazepines are avoided where possible in pregnancy (check the SPC), and pregnancy itself raises VTE risk. RCOG guidance on reducing the risk of VTE in pregnancy treats long-distance travel (over 4 hours) as a transient risk factor; with additional risk factors such as age over 35, BMI 30 or more, an IVF pregnancy or a family history of VTE, an individual assessment is needed and thromboprophylaxis may be advised by the maternity team. General travel advice in pregnancy: mobilise and do calf exercises, stay hydrated, avoid alcohol, wear well-fitted graduated compression stockings, choose an aisle seat, carry maternity notes, and check that travel insurance covers pregnancy; airlines may ask for a letter later in pregnancy (often after 28 weeks). Non-drug approaches to flight anxiety include slow breathing, grounding, distraction, telling the crew and, longer term, CBT-based courses. The hidden agenda is acute grief complicated by guilt after an estranged parent’s sudden death, with panic attacks: acknowledge it, assess mood and risk, offer bereavement support and NHS Talking Therapies, and follow up on return. Holding a prescribing boundary is easier when the patient feels heard and leaves with a better plan than the one she came for.

model.text: Hello, is that Bianca Foster? I’m Dr Clarke. Can you confirm your date of birth, and are you somewhere you can talk?
Yes. I just need a quick prescription. I’ve got a long-haul flight on Saturday and I can’t do it without a few diazepam. My old GP always gave them. Five would do.
Thanks for explaining. Before I think about medicines, I can see from your notes you’re pregnant. How far along are you, and how are you both doing?
About 15 weeks. Fine, I think. I didn’t think it mattered for this.
It does matter, and we’ll come to that. It sounds like this trip came up quickly. Can I ask what it’s for?
(pause, tearful) My dad died. On Tuesday. In Toronto. The funeral’s next week.
I’m so sorry, Bianca. That’s a huge shock. How are you coping?
Not well. We hadn’t spoken for three years. We fell out. I kept meaning to ring him. Now I can’t.
That guilt makes grief so much heavier. Have you been having panic attacks, trouble sleeping or eating? And have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?
Panic attacks every day. I can’t sleep. No, I wouldn’t hurt myself, I’ve got the baby.
Thank you for telling me. And the flying, what happens for you?
Bad turbulence years ago. Since then I panic as soon as the doors close.
What were you hoping the diazepam would do?
Knock me out so I sleep through it. And I’m scared all this stress is bad for the baby.

That makes sense. I’m not going to prescribe diazepam, and I want to explain why, because it’s about keeping you and the baby safe. We avoid it in pregnancy where we can. Sleeping still for hours raises the risk of a clot in the legs, and that risk is already higher in pregnancy and on long flights. And if anything happened on the plane, you’d need to be alert.
It’s only five tablets.
I know it feels small. But I think we can make the flight more manageable in other ways, and do something about the clot risk at the same time.
Have you had any clots, or anyone in the family?
My mum had one after an operation.

With a flight of eight hours, your pregnancy after IVF, your weight and your mum’s clot, I’d like the maternity team to assess you before Saturday in case you need blood-thinning injections for the journey. I’ll contact your midwife today. On the plane: an aisle seat, walk every hour, calf exercises, plenty of water and no alcohol, and flight socks.

For the panic: breathe in for four, out for six, and name five things you can see. Tell the crew you’re a nervous flyer, they’re used to it. There are free apps and courses for fear of flying, which you could look at for the future.
Take your maternity notes, and check your travel insurance covers pregnancy. If you get bleeding, tummy pain or a painful swollen leg or chest pain while away, get seen urgently there.
And for the grief, I’d like to see you when you’re back. Bereavement services and NHS Talking Therapies can help, and you can self-refer. Is that okay?
Can you tell me what you’ll do before Saturday?
Midwife about the clot thing. Flight socks, aisle seat, water, walk. Breathing. Notes and insurance. See you when I’m back.
Exactly. If the panic becomes unbearable, or you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, call us, 111, or Samaritans on 116 123. I’m really sorry about your dad.

social.t: Sudden travel for a funeral adds cost, stress and logistics. Estrangement adds guilt and complicates grief.
Women who conceived after IVF often carry extra anxiety about anything that might affect the pregnancy.

legal.t: Some countries restrict benzodiazepines; travellers may need documentation. Another reason to avoid prescribing for flights.
The prescriber is responsible for the decision, whatever a previous doctor did (GMC prescribing guidance).

professional.t: Many practices have a policy on benzodiazepines for flights. Explaining the clinical reasons matters more than citing policy.
Ask about pregnancy before prescribing for any woman of reproductive age.

community.t: Cruse Bereavement Support and local services; NHS Talking Therapies self-referral.
Airlines and providers run CBT-based courses; useful for future travel.
